title: The God Who Makes Bitter Things Sweet
source: Banner of Truth · 教会历史
summary: The Israelites had just walked between the walls of the water of the Red Sea and watched as the Lord washed away the whole Egyptian army. They sang a song of triumph on the far shore of the sea, rejoicing in the fear that had fallen on the surrounding nations (Ex. 15:14-16) and looking forward […]   The post  The God Who Makes Bitter Things Sweet  appeared first on  Banner of Truth USA .
content: The Israelites had just walked between the walls of the water of the Red Sea and watched as the Lord washed away the whole Egyptian army. They sang a song of triumph on the far shore of the sea, rejoicing in the fear that had fallen on the surrounding nations (Ex. 15:14-16) and looking forward to taking possession of the Promised Land in the near future (Ex. 15:17). But within three days they raised a very different kind of sound—a chorus of grumbling against Moses because there was no water to drink at Marah (Ex. 15:22-26). I wonder what they expected would happen after the Red Sea. A straight, unhindered journey to the land flowing with milk and honey? Instead the first thing the Lord does is to lead his people to the undrinkable water of Marah. There is no question that the Lord is the one who led them there—it is easy enough to take a wrong turn when you are following Google Maps, but not when you are following a towering pillar of cloud or fire! So why did God lead Israel to Marah? Is it because he is sadistic and cruel and takes delight in watching his people suffer dehydration and fear? Is it because he is really bad at geography? Of course not! In fact we’re told why he brought Israel to Marah in Ex. 15:25: There the Lord tested them. In fact, the whole wilderness is a place of testing. That’s the significance of the wilderness—it’s a hard place. Deuteronomy 8:15 calls it ‘the vast and dreadful wilderness, that thirsty and waterless land, with its venomous snakes and scorpions.’ God is training his infant son to trust him—and training is always painful. There are no short cuts, whether in the physical training of our bodies to make them stronger and faster, or in the mental training of our minds to increase our knowledge and understanding, or in the spiritual training of our souls to grow in godliness. Learning to trust God is not something we can do lounging on the sofa. It means being put into situations that are stressful, confusing, messy and complicated, when we don’t understand what is going on or see any answers. Anyone can trust God when things are easy; the real test is if you will trust God when things are tough. Israel’s failure Marah was Israel’s first test and they failed. They have been travelling for three days and haven’t found any water. Supplies are running low. Perhaps as they saw the waters of Marah in the distance they finished up their last reserves: ‘It’ll be OK—we can refill very soon!’ Imagine the relief and joy as the first to reach Marah fall down and scoop the water to their mouths. And imagine them spitting it out as they discover it is foul and undrinkable. They’re not just disappointed—they’re horrified . Panic seizes them. ‘What shall we drink?’ (v. 24) This is not like someone in a restaurant complaining that their steak is a bit on the tough side or that the soup is a tad cold. They are exhausted and dehydrated and they can’t see any way of getting water. Suddenly life is hanging by a thread. There is nothing unreasonable about their concern. That is not why they fail the test. They fail the test because of their attitude. They grumble: the word means ‘hostile complaining, verbal attacks of dissatisfied people.’ Why do they grumble? There are at least two reasons: Faithlessness . They do not trust God. They don’t trust his power (that he can take care of them) or his goodness (that he wants to take care of them). They should have gone to the Lord with their needs, humbly asking him to provide what they needed. And this lack of faith was due to… Forgetfulness . This is the diagnosis of Psalm 78:40ff: How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert! … They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe , 43 when he performed his signs in Egypt and his marvels in the fields of Zoan. The people had such short memories! It has only been three days since they walked through the Red Sea! It has been just a few weeks since they witn

content: Faith Cook’s Troubled Journey narrates her early experiences as the daughter of OMF missionaries to China. Honouring the faith, courage, and self-sacrifice of her parents, she also shines a compassionate light on the family deprivations brought about by long periods of separation from them. The excerpt below is Chapter 11 of the book in question, which cover Faith’s childhood between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. A passage on the P & O Carthage was booked for Stanley and Norah [Faith’s parents—Ed.] in early January 1952, only eight months after our family had first arrived back from China. It was a subdued Christmas we spent together that year, the last for some years to come. Frantic packing followed, purchasing school uniform and preparing for the long outward journey back to the Far East, this time by sea. A round of speaking engagements filled the days for my parents and seemingly eased the ache of the forthcoming separation. As the day of parting drew ever nearer, I noticed a new tenderness in their attitude towards me – a tenderness that only added to my distress. And at last came the day of departure. It would be four years before we would see them again. Photographs were taken on the steps of the mission headquarters, as all joined to wish the departing missionaries well. Norah’s expression told a story, as did fifteen-year-old Christopher’s forced smile, for in reality, the boy’s spirit was at breaking point. On we went to the station where our parents would board a train to Southampton. A large contingent of missionary personnel followed, for this departure was highly significant for the entire future of the mission, urgently seeking a new role for its operations now the door to China was closed. I found myself thrust to the back of the crowd as the train slowly moved off. Suddenly one more thoughtful friend spotted the irony of the situation and pushed me to the front to catch the last glimpse of my parents as they stood waving at the window of the train, my mother looking tense and tearful, and my father strained. Back at the mission home once more, we were at a loose end. No guardian had yet been appointed to care for us, although one or two kindly adults helped out if I asked for assistance. The Spring term would soon begin and I was glad. Some of my new clothes were too long and needed altering, and I discovered with alarm that the shoe repairer considered my school shoes beyond his skills to patch up. Never handy with a needle, I tried my best to turn up the hems myself. At last the third week of January arrived and I was on the train back to my well-loved school – a place I now regarded as home. Although soon immersed once more in all the trivia of boarding school life, I found time each week to write a letter to my parents. The first few letters were addressed to ports en route for Malaysia where the P & O Carthage would call: Aden, Penang and then to Singapore to await their arrival. Stanley and Norah treasured these schoolgirl epistles, storing them all up, until at last my father would present his married daughter with a shoe box crammed with letters dating from January 1952 until the time that he and my mother finally retired from missionary service in Malaysia more than twenty years later. These letters form a unique commentary on the development of a postal relationship with my parents that would form the bedrock of my security and development from a young teenager to womanhood and beyond. Faithfully my parents replied to each letter, commenting on my progress, chiding when they could sense my behaviour was becoming erratic, and offering advice as well as they were able. Not long after arriving back at the mission headquarters in London at the end of the spring school term, I discovered that a middle-aged couple had been appointed as guardians for the children of the missionaries: Louis and Nancy Gaussen. Understanding and kindly, they were well-suited to care for the children. ‘Mr and Mrs Gaussen

title: In the Christian Life There is No Necessary Crisis Experience
source: Banner of Truth · 教会历史
summary: The fourth of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. There is no crisis experience promised or commanded as an essential element in living the Christian life. Some teaching on the Christian life asserts that […]   The post  In the Christian Life There is No Necessary Crisis Experience  appeared first on  Banner of Truth USA .
content: The fourth of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. There is no crisis experience promised or commanded as an essential element in living the Christian life. Some teaching on the Christian life asserts that only a low level of Christian experience can be realized by the person who has not had a crisis experience subsequent to regeneration, or at least subsequent to conversion and to the beginning of conscious Christian experience. Furthermore, it is asserted that the crisis experience is both commanded and promised by God as the entrance into a qualitatively new dimension or level of spiritual experience, reality and power. Throughout the history of the Christian church there have been many different strands of this crisis teaching. There is what we might call ‘classic Wesleyan perfectionism,’ which concentrated particularly upon sanctification and spoke of a baptism of purifying fire, or of coming into a state of perfect love. It concentrated not so much on power for service or upon inward feelings, but on a crisis experience in which the power of indwelling sin was to all intents and purposes negated. I have read enough of classic Wesleyan theology to know that there are different opinions as to what John Wesley himself taught on the subject. But in a general descriptive manner this, I believe, is an accurate representation of old-style classic Wesleyan perfectionism. Then, too, there is ‘the old Pentecostalism’ in which the emphasis was upon a baptism in the Holy Spirit, generally subsequent to conversion, and invariably manifested by speaking in tongues: the way you knew that you had this baptism of power was that, when it came to you, you spoke in tongues. The primary focus in old classic Pentecostalism was the matter of power for service. Thirdly, there is the modern ‘charismatic movement.’ Like classic Pentecostalism, its teachers use many of the same passages in the Book of Acts to support their theory of this necessary crisis. So they emphasize that in most cases—although there are different schools among modern charismatics—it will be manifested by the speaking in tongues. Some are content to believe you have ‘got it’ if you have a season of holy laughter. Others, however, say that you have not spoken in tongues because you have some psychological hold-ups, and if these can be removed the tongues are there. You just have not given them utterance. Here the emphasis is not so much on a baptism of purifying fire (as in the case of old classic Wesleyan perfectionism), or the baptism of power (as in the case of old classic Pentecostalism), but more upon a baptism of joyful praise-filled experience. I have been speaking of generalities, but I believe they are accurate. Fourthly, there are the various forms of ‘higher life’ teaching. What they have in common is this: you are simply converted, simply united to Christ, simply regenerated, and then you come to a crisis of surrender and faith, in which ‘you let go and let God’ and appropriate the indwelling life of Christ. The common denominator is that it is a crisis without any external manifestation of tongues or holy laughter or shouting or jumping, but the end result will be new power to live a holy life—the emphasis falls upon the ability to be more efficient in the path of holiness. Fifthly, there is a kind of teaching which has both old and modern proponents. It focuses on assurance, and has been expressed in terms of the biblical language of a ‘sealing of the Holy Spirit.’ Some of the Puritans—Thomas Goodwin, for example—taught this. There have been certain preachers in our own day who have believed this very strongly and emphasized it repeatedly. title: Amy Carmichael: Times of Refreshing and Times of Trial
source: Banner of Truth · 教会历史
summary: Iain H. Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes is a short retelling of the remarkable life of the Irish missionary to India. What follows is Chapter 4 of that title, ‘Hard Days and Golden Years.’ If there was any pattern to Amy Carmichael’s life it was of times of refreshing then of trials, of exhilarating ‘climbing’ […]   The post  Amy Carmichael: Times of Refreshing and Times of Trial  appeared first on  Banner of Truth USA .
content: Iain H. Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes is a short retelling of the remarkable life of the Irish missionary to India. What follows is Chapter 4 of that title, ‘Hard Days and Golden Years.’ If there was any pattern to Amy Carmichael’s life it was of times of refreshing then of trials, of exhilarating ‘climbing’ then of walking in dark ravines. In part her explanation was that demonic activity follows the work of the Holy Spirit. As she quoted from George Bowen, When Christianity assumes an aggressive attitude the first result is a great exhibition of Satanic power. Satan’s power to be manifested must be assaulted. 1 Such an understanding does not come so readily to us who do not live, as she did, within sight of demon possession, or within hearing of tom-tom drums calling devotees to idols. Shortly before Walker 2 had left on his last mission, he had been sitting with Amy and others in deck chairs under the stars. ‘We had been talking’, she later wrote, of work and workers, and of those (to me) most wonderful women, who seemed perfectly self-reliant, needing no strong arm alongside. I remember how, suddenly startled at the bare thought of working alone, in the sense of all the burden of responsibility, I exclaimed that I never could do it. Mr Walker laughed. ‘Well, you don’t have to’, he said. 3 Amy was the weaker when her ‘strong arm’ died at the age of fifty-four. What she owed to Walker’s ‘courageous championship’ of the children’s work, ‘through its first very difficult years, no words can tell, nor can words tell how he is missed’. 4 At times, as she faced her loss, she would need to say to herself, ‘Don’t give up, don’t be afraid: go on.’ Prayer for ‘fortitude’ entered her life. There were unsympathetic neighbours who observed the work at Dohnavur who supposed that Amy would now be more vulnerable. One of these was a lawyer who, soon after Walker’s death, wrote with the demand that current work on the building of a wall around the compoundbe stopped, and that a half-built nursery should be pulled down. They were using ground, he claimed, to which they did not have legal title. ‘He had waited till Mr Walker’s death had left us, as he thought, defenceless, almost desolate, and sure to be easily cowed by threats of court trouble.’ The wall building had been prompted by the passage of a tiger through the compound at night; and the new nursery was necessitated by the growing numbers of children for whom Dohnavur had become home. Amy ignored the letter and heard nothing more of the threat. The Dohnavur family of seventy children and grown-ups in 1906, had doubled itself by this date, and the need of more helpers was pressing. Mrs Catherine Carmichael was never able to return. She died on July 14, 1913. A few weeks earlier a letter from her to Amy began with the words, ‘My own most precious earthly possession’. While Amy did not lament her mother’s death—for no Christian death was to be ‘lamented’—in the days ahead she needed to preach to herself, ‘I must remind myself to live in the joy of those gone, not grovel in the sense of my loss.’ Mrs Carmichael had been a constant supporter and representative for Dohnavur in Britain. She acted as the home secretary to whom gifts could be sent, and helped to make her daughter’s books more widely known. In 1912 those books had been noted by Queen Mary, wife of King George V, who expressed her thanks for them. While Amy was busy in 1913 writing Walker of Tinnevelly , there came the possibility of the loss of her closest female friend and helper, Ponnammal, who had been with her ever since, as a young widow, she had come to new life through Walker’s preaching. She now needed surgery for cancer and Amy went with her to a Salvation Army Hospital at Neyyoor for a period. content: The second of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. Principle 2: There is no escape from tension and conflict in living the Christian life. I do not say that the Christian life is all tension and all conflict. The kind of teaching I am attempting to expose as fallacious is as follows: At a conference a speaker takes a text out of context to which he attaches or from which he extracts a shibboleth – perhaps the shibboleth of Christ living his life through us, or the saving life of Christ, or the abiding life. Then the preacher, having expounded his theory of the Christian life, gives an appeal like this: ‘Child of God, are you weary of the tension of wrestling with your remaining sin? Are you tired of struggling in prayer? Are you weary of having to battle with impure thoughts and thoughts of envy and pride and jealousy? Are you tired of this incessant conflict?’ And every true Christian sits there with his fangs dripping, saying, ‘Oh God, you know I am tired, I would give anything to have one day, one day in which I did not have to battle with dullness of heart and distraction of mind and the seductions to sin that come from without and from within’. And the speaker then says ‘Ah, if you are tired of the tension, weary of the conflict, if you will but take these steps, then Christ will so live his life through you that it will be a life marked by the negation of tension and conflict. You will be so filled with the Spirit, so taken up in the Spirit, that tension and conflict for all intents and purposes will be a thing of the past as long as you maintain the posture of the abiding life. The moment you feel tension and conflict, it is because you slipped out of that life, back to your old ways.’ Now that is not a caricature, that is spelled out in page after page, book after book. Beware of the writings of Watchman Nee! Beware of some of the writings of such as Norman Grubb and Hannah Whithall Smith. Beware of these writings, because if you take them seriously they could drive you either into a world of unreality or into a world of scepticism. Now what proof do I offer from the word of God for that proposition? 1. Because of the reality of indwelling sin with its incessant and powerful actions upon us. Galatians 5:17: ‘The flesh is lusting against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh and these two are contrary the one to the other, so that you may not do the things that you would’. And Paul does not go on to say that there is a way to be utterly, totally delivered from that conscious­ness of tension and conflict. He does tell us that we need not be dominated by the flesh: ‘Walk in the Spirit and you shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh’. But he nowhere says that the consciousness of the flesh’s lusting will be negated, and where flesh is lusting against Spirit, there is conflict. title: Spoiled for Choice: Two New Graphic Novels of Pilgrim’s Progress
summary: Two new graphic novel adaptations of Pilgrim’s Progress have arrived within weeks of each other. Here's how they are similar and different, and my recommendation of which one to buy. See Also A La Carte (July 27) The Puritans: John Bunyan A La Carte (6/3)
content: I have often expressed how spoiled Christian readers are today. As if we needed more proof of this, how about the fact that in a single month, publishers released not one but two major graphic novel adaptations of Pilgrim’s Progress ? Both are well-written, beautifully illustrated, and faithful to Bunyan’s story. Let me help you understand their similarities and differences and tell you which one might be best to add to your library. Christian’s Quest is written by Tyler Van Halteren and illustrated by Manuel Zepic. It is published by Lithos Kids, which has already released the three-part Little Pilgrim’s Big Journey , an illustrated adaptation of Pilgrim’s Progress for young readers, and The Mansoul Chronicles , which is based on Bunyan’s Holy War . It is a 220-page 7×10.63 inch hardcover that targets children aged 8+, though it is meant to be enjoyed by teens and adults as well. Its illustrations are what I might describe as a clean, polished YA style. The lines are thin and tidy and much of the form comes from shading. The colors tend to maintain a soft, muted, painted look. It lightly updates some antiquated language so that Bunyan’s Slough of Despond becomes the Bog of Despond. Christian is youthful and fresh-faced, and his burden is a bulging pack on a frame. It includes some bonus material: a behind-the-scenes look at how a graphic novel is made, and a study guide that explains and applies each of the stages of Christian’s quest. It also indicates that a sequel, Christiana’s Crown , will be released in 2028. Pilgrim’s Progress: The Graphic Novel is written by Jeremy Patenaude, illustrated by Brent McKee, colored by Matt Wilson, and lettered by Taylor Esposito. It is published by Crossway as what I believe is the company’s first graphic novel, though it has a long history of publishing books for young readers. It is a 256-page 7×10.25 inch paperback that targets readers aged 14+. Its illustrations are what I might describe as gritty and stylized and perhaps a bit more indie than mainstream. It uses heavy brush ink, dark shadows, and vivid colors. It does not update Bunyan’s antiquated language. Christian is a gaunt, tormented, weathered adult whose burden is a huge stone roped to his back. Its bonus material includes a lexicon of the key characters and locations and reflections on each of the chapters. There is no indication of a sequel that will cover Christiana’s quest. While these two graphic novels tell the same story and tell it faithfully using dialogue and illustration rather than narration, they tell it using different visual language largely because Christian’s Quest is meant to be accessible to a younger demographic. You might say that Christian’s Quest is a bit more kid-friendly and Pilgrim’s Progress is a bit more adult-friendly, though both could easily be enjoyed by kids and adults alike. After all, who doesn’t enjoy reading the occasional graphic novel? Another key difference is that Pilgrim’s Progress is a paperback where Christian’s Quest is being sold as more of an heirloom object that features cloth binding, gold foil, and a ribbon marker. Let me show you a few examples of the art from each book. Christian’s Quest These are drawn from the publisher’s preview images. Pilgrim’s Progress These are drawn from the sample chapter on Crossway’s site. My Recommendation Which do I recommend? Either! Both! If your readers are younger, Christian’s Quest is the more obvious choice, and if they are older—teenagers and up—they may prefer Pilgrim’s Progress . But you couldn’t go wrong with either, and you couldn’t go wrong with picking up both. Where to Buy Christian’s Quest Lithos Kids · clothbound hardcover · ages 8+ Buy at Amazon Westminster Books Pilgrim’s Progress: The Graphic Novel Crossway · paperback · ages 14+ Buy at Amazon Westminster Books See Also A La Carte (July 27) The Puritans: John Bunyan A La Carte (6/3)

title: A La Carte (November 12)
summary: On spouses sitting together in church / Can’t you just be like me? / Husbands, pray for your wives / Six comforts for pastors / The most fun I ever had / Will we really be perfect in heaven? / The most offensive doctrine / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (October 7) A La Carte (September 3) A La Carte (August 1)
content: I hope you don’t mind that this is a bit of a book-heavy week, but I’ve had a lot of book content I have wanted to share. Hence, we’ve had This Week in Christian Books , The First 100 Books for the Children’s Section of Your Church Library , and Spoiled for Choice: Two New Graphic Novels of Pilgrim’s Progress . A book review will follow tomorrow, then we’ll be mostly caught up for now. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include P rioritizing the Church in Missions , Growing Up , and several good books for children. Recommended Reading On Spouses Sitting Together in Church. I happened to spot some of the kerfuffle that erupted after TGC Australia shared an article about why spouses should consider not sitting together in church. As happens on social media, the response seemed far out of proportion to the article. I found Murray Campbell’s response a good and reasonable one, even if I intend to keep sitting with Aileen most Sundays. Can’t You Just Be Like Me? I suppose in some ways, Bobby Scott’s piece on tribalism and disunity could nicely follow the previous article. “Tribalistic churches and Christians demand conformity to their broad range of preferences, believing they are inviolable God-ordained principles. So they strive to silence or coerce other Christians to assimilate, or they quietly despise these brothers and sisters. This inevitably leads to dark consequences. Instead of loving other Christians who have the same primary biblical convictions but differ over tertiary issues, tribalistic Christians feel justified in waging war against them.” Nelson’s Complete Book of Bible Maps and Charts is out in a fourth edition, updated with new high-resolution photography to go with its full-color maps, timelines, and charts for every book of the Bible. (Sponsored) Husbands, Pray for Your Wives. Costi Hinn: “I’ll never forget the first time I sat in a men’s Bible study on a Saturday morning listening to a man unpack the importance of praying for your wife. I was honestly blown away by the simplicity of it all and how I had never thought to pray for her — and I mean, like really pray for her.” He outlines eight ways men can do so. Six Comforts for Pastors. This article from Darryl Dash delivers what it promises. “If we base our identity on how well our ministries are going from an earthly perspective, we will be in trouble. Every pastor’s ministry will have good times and bad times. Basing our identity on how well things seem to be going is like putting our hope in a volatile stock. We will end up elated some of the time and despondent the rest. As pastors, we need to put our confidence in something more secure than how well things seem to be going. Here are six comforts for pastors that will last and sustain us, no matter how well or poorly our ministry seems to be going.” The Most Fun I Ever Had. Concerned about all those who are disparaging motherhood today, Brittany Allen chooses to celebrate it. “I still find it hard to write articles about the joys of motherhood because I never want to isolate sisters who are longing for a family. Yet, at the same time, I want to talk back to our culture that treats motherhood as a curse rather than a gift.” Will We Really Be Perfect in Heaven? Randy Alcorn: “Someone e-mailed me this question: ‘In Heaven, will some people still be annoying? After all, eternity’s a long time!’ Annoyance is sometimes caused by others’ sin, our own, or both. Since sin will be eliminated, so will annoyance. That doesn’t mean people won’t have idiosyncrasies, only that they won’t be rooted in sin, and none of us will degrade or dismiss others.” He explains what it means that we will be perfect in heaven. The Most Offensive Doctrine Every now and again, I like to share a quote that I have encountered through my reading. This is drawn from J.C. Ryle’s Expository Thoughts on Luke , which I’m enjoying a lot. Of all the doctrines of the Bible, none is so offensive to human nature as the doctrine of God’s sovereignty.

summary: A new serpent in the garden of Africa / On naming the dead / Why your favorite worship song’s grammar matters / 3 Reasons you should not date while watching porn / Would you forgive me of my narcissism? / Christianity Today and the sin of centrism / Kindle deals, videos, and more See Also A La Carte (June 27) Weekend A La Carte (October 25) Kindle Deals for Christian Readers
content: Good morning, my friends. The God of love and peace be with you today. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include Paul Tripp & Timothy Lane’s excellent Relationships: A Mess Worth Making , R.C. Sproul’s Growing in Holiness (which I don’t think I’ve seen on sale before), and Jonathan Landry Cruse’s What Happens When We Worship , among others. If you’d like to celebrate Advent with Spurgeon, Westminster Books has a deal on a new devotional book that may be of interest to you. If that’s not quite right for you, there’s lots of other resources in the Advent Sale . Recommended Reading A New Serpent in the Garden of Africa. “Just as the serpent led Adam and Eve into idolatry by reinterpreting God’s good word, so prosperity and word-of-faith preachers are today proclaiming a false and idolatrous gospel. But unlike Adam, African preachers are refusing to stay mute. Recognizing the need for faithful interpretation of Scripture, they have drawn up a statement to help pastors stand against the idolatrous assumptions and teachings of the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith theology.” Dieudonné Tamfu writes from an African perspective and describes the importance of the recent Africa Statement on the Prosperity Gospel and Word of Faith Theology . On Naming the Dead. Andrew Roycroft explains why it’s important that we not merely remember the dead, but name them. “The park bench copperplate, the trinkets and human ephemera that we treasure more than diamonds, the ongoing dedication of certain pieces of music truly matter, and keep back the dimming power of death for a time. Recently, in the wake of my friend’s death, I have been seeking to honour him by reading his favourite authors, enjoying afresh what I know he enjoyed and feeling a continued sense of fraternity and fellowship through these authors who meant so much to him.” Why Your Favorite Worship Song’s Grammar Matters. Porter C. Taylor explains why grammar matters when it comes to worship songs, and why the Psalms model the kind of worship that serves us best. “What if the worship wars have been fighting the wrong battle? What if contemporary worship music supplies a necessary register too often missing from our musical praise before our Creator? The question we should ask of our worship songs is not simply whether they make accurate statements about God. We should also ask what they enable the gathered church to say and do before God.” Nelson’s Complete Book of Bible Maps and Charts is out in a fourth edition, updated with new high-resolution photography to go with its full-color maps, timelines, and charts for every book of the Bible.  (Sponsored) 3 Reasons You Should Not Date While Watching Porn. I don’t think I am the only one who has been asked this question many times over: Should I refrain from dating until I am free from porn? Jacob Valk answers in the affirmative and offers three good reasons. Would You Forgive Me of My Narcissism? John Beeson explains why narcissism may not just be a problem that others have. “The most discussed personality disorder of our day is narcissism. A brief foray into Google Trends (always a fun rabbit hole to go down) shows that through the early 2000s, narcissism was searched about as often as some of the more well-known personality disorders. In 2015, that number began to rise and by 2022, it rocketed way above any other psychiatric disorder search. That aligns with my own experience as it is now a regular occurrence for me to hear a counselee accuse someone else of narcissism.” Christianity Today and the Sin of Centrism. Nicholas McDonald read the news about Christianity Today ‘s recent struggles and “the whole thing got me thinking about centrism in general, and why, by itself, trying to be ‘centrist’ falls short of what it means to do Christian ethics.” Videos Worth Watching Here are a few brief videos that caught my attention this week: John Piper on Christian Nationalism. title: This Week in Christian Books (November 10, 2026)
summary: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books. Here is a look at the Christian books that came our way this week, including Biblical and Theological Studies, From Silence to Sinai. See Also New and Notable Christian Books for October 2026 (Plus a Preview of November) This Week in Christian Books (October 27, 2026) Best Commentaries on Leviticus
content: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books, so each week I like to let you know what has just come our way from the publishers I follow most closely. It is a quieter week than the last one, but it brings a revised edition of B. B. Warfield’s Biblical and Theological Studies, Alex Duke’s guided tour of Exodus (for which I provided a foreword), and two Crossway editions marking 500 years since William Tyndale’s English New Testament. On the academic side, you’ll find several noteworthy titles, including the New International Commentary on the Old Testament volume on Daniel 7–12. In each case, I’ve included the publisher’s description. Books for Everyone Zondervan From Silence to Sinai A Guided Tour of Exodus Alex Duke Publisher’s description What adjectives would you use to describe the Bible? Inspired. Amazing. Unique. Authoritative. Perfect. Pure. Life-changing. Those descriptions are all deserved. Your pastors and parents and Sunday School teachers were right. There’s no book like God’s Book. Here’s another adjective: confusing. The Bible can be confusing, especially certain parts of the Old Testament. Moments after coming across something inspiring and encouraging, you’ll read something that makes you wonder, What is even happening right now!? The book of Exodus is no exception. This sequel to Genesis begins with God’s surprising silence. What a stark contrast to Genesis, where God’s words set everything in motion. It then tells the story of God’s miraculous liberation of his people, complete with frogs falling from the sky and life-saving blood being painted over doorways. Finally, for the last half of the book, the action slows down as the people of God gather at the mountain of God to receive the Law of God in order to engage in the worship of God. From silence to Sinai, that’s the story of Exodus. To understand it all, most of us will need a guide. We’ll need some help. That’s what From Silence to Sinai is for. Alex Duke walks readers through the book of Exodus to show that nothing in God’s story is wasted—not the silence, not the ten signs, and not even the confusing parts. In Exodus, God is not absent, random, or unclear. He is revealing himself, redeeming his people, and teaching them how to live in his presence. Buy it at Amazon or Westminster Books . In The First Five , Joseph and Kyle Worley present a pathway for thriving in ministry leadership. With over sixty years of experience, across churches of every size and shape, they provide a biblically rooted and tested approach to the personal, professional, and pastoral dynamics of ministry leadership. The First Five is designed to be a manual for new ministry leaders and those leading them. Don’t just read this book—use it! You can do more than survive as a ministry leader. title: A La Carte (November 10)
summary: C.S. Lewis's vices / How to graciously say no / Can’t you let me just attend? / When morningness is confused with godliness / Everyone doesn’t react the same way / Evangelizing with a dog / Kindle deals / New books See Also A La Carte (1/12) A La Carte (11/10) A La Carte (12/2)
content: Let me take a moment to remind you of some of the features of this site you may not know about. I have a growing page of Liturgies meant to help the local church in its worship. I also offer Book Recommendations across many categories and a list of the Best Commentaries for each book of the Bible. And if you like the quote graphics I share day by day, you can find them all at SquareQuotes.church where they are free to download. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include several of the “Heart Talks” mini books that are meant to help women with common concerns: feeling like failures in parenting, husbands who lead poorly, doubt, and so on. You’ll also find Greg Gifford’s Lies My Therapist Told Me and several other titles. Recommended Reading Beer, Beef and Player’s Navy Cut. This is a brilliant article about C.S. Lewis and the vices that dogged him throughout his life—a three-pack-a day smoking habit, eating habits that bordered on gluttony, and far more alcohol than anyone should consume. “In case you really are new here and you mostly know Lewis from the kid’s books, let’s state the obvious: the man we universally honor as one of the 20th Century’s great saints smoked, ate and drank like he was a sponsored athlete of consumption. He sinned frequently through overindulgence. What do we do with this information?” How to Graciously Say No. You have probably run into the same conclusion I have: it’s often far harder to say no than to say yes. Yet sometimes the best thing we can do for ourselves and for others is to say no. Reagan Rose offers some thoughts on that (for those who have the ability to say no, of course, since in many occupations saying no isn’t an option). Can’t You Let Me Just Attend? “We live in a chronically noncommittal society. No wonder, then, that this has been dubbed the age of anxiety. Surely, covenant relationships aren’t the only cure, but it might surprise us how much stability of soul comes from deep, reliable, unflighty fellowship.” David Mathis explains why commitment to a particular church is so important, even if it’s extremely countercultural. When Morningness Is Confused With Godliness. I always enjoy an article that provides an alternate view of something we almost take for granted. That’s the case with this one from Cole Mizel, who is concerned that we may be too quick to imply that the best Christians do their daily devotions in the morning. “But is it really more virtuous to be a morning person than a night owl?” Everyone Doesn’t React the Same Way. J.V. Fesko makes a simple but wise point here: everyone doesn’t respond to preaching the same way. Because that’s the case, we should not assume that those who display a lot of emotion are necessarily being impacted more than those who do not. “Tears are not the sacrament of a changed heart, the visible sign and seal of an anguished and healed soul.” Evangelising With a Dog. I enjoyed reading Peter Barnes’s account of evangelizing with a dog. “My doctor, who is half my size, suggested as tactfully as he could, what was obvious to all – that my squash days were over, and that I should take to walking the dog in the morning and at lunchtime. So this has become my nod to the need for daily exercise. Being one of the few beings on the planet who still buys a hard copy of a daily newspaper, I take my hound – a cocker spaniel with unusually short legs – with me of a morning. title: Why Many Profess Christ but Don’t Possess Christ—and What It Means for Discipleship
summary: The gospel still changes everything. But have we embraced something less? The reason many profess Christ but don't possess Christ, and how a reduced understanding of the gospel can leave people mistaking religious activity for saving faith. See Also The Hard Work Is Done—Family Bible Study Is Fun Free-stuff Fridays (Truth78) Evangelize 2024: Growing a Church That Proclaims The Gospel
content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Moody Publishers and adapted from The Unstoppable Gospel by Karl Clauson. It’s impossible to disciple lost people. That sounds obvious. Maybe too obvious to even say out loud. But when the church dilutes or neglects the good news, devastation is left in its wake. After forty years of ministry, this is the most sobering truth I’ve learned about the Western church: We do not merely have a discipleship problem today. We have a gospel problem. Before we ever became weak at disciple-making, we began redefining conversion itself. We slowly traded supernatural regeneration for human decision. Salvation became a prayer to repeat, a card to sign, an aisle to walk, while millions were assured of heaven without ever being transformed by the power of God. We didn’t offer them a belief lacking power, we offered them a powerless belief. The result is a generation that has been deeply Christianized but not necessarily changed. They know the language. They know the songs. They know when to stand, when to sit, when to say amen. They have been immersed in church culture, yet many have never been brought from death to life. We have filled churches with people who have learned how to function in and around “Christianity” without ever truly following Christ. And when that happens, discipleship collapses under the weight of human effort. When evangelism centers on human decision, discipleship inevitably becomes self-powered. Following Jesus is reduced to behavior management, moral striving, and “try harder next time.” The supernatural life Christ promised is replaced with self-help dressed up in religious garb. Dallas Willard spoke of “the Great Omission,” the church’s failure to make disciples. He was right. But I believe something even deeper has happened. Before we omitted discipleship, we compromised the very gospel that births disciples in the first place. That is the crisis. That is the great deception. And until we recover the true faith that changes everything, we will continue trying to disciple people who have never truly been made alive. We have, sitting in our church chairs and pews every weekend—even in good, Bible-teaching churches—vast numbers of people who believe themselves to be saved but possess no power beyond their own efforts and whose lives show only surface evidence of new birth. People assume what they have is all God has for them, not knowing they are cultural Christians, so close yet so far from God. People who have been taught a version of Christianity divorced from repentance, from surrender, from the cost of discipleship and, tragically, from the power that makes the gospel unstoppable. Many profess Christ but don’t possess Christ. We’ve left people needing more, wanting more, and settling for too little. The great deception must end. There is life for the spiritually dead. There is surrender that leads to life instead of loss. There is repentance that produces the rhythm of a flourishing soul. There is discipline that flows from grace instead of fear or performance. And there is deep, liberating, unmistakable freedom when Christ becomes everything. This is why truth must be championed. Not as an idea, but as a reality that cuts, clarifies, and calls us forward. Because when truth becomes really clear, it doesn’t just inform you. It changes you. It brings you out of the fog, out of the confusion, out of the illusion—and into a life that is grounded, whole, and fully alive with God. This is the gospel that birthed the early church. This is the gospel that turned the world upside down. This is the gospel that sustains God’s kids under brutal persecution today. This is the gospel the church has forgotten and the good news it desperately needs. This is the gospel that still changes everything today. Learn more about how we’ve embraced a version of the gospel that falls short of the life Jesus promised, and how you can go from powerless belief to a true faith that changes everything. Get

title: What If Your Church Sings Hillsong and You Wish It Wouldn’t?
summary: A few weeks ago, I explained why my church does not sing songs by Hillsong, and, by the same convictions, songs by Bethel and Elevation. Today, a related matter: what should you do if your church sings Hillsong, but you wish it wouldn’t? See Also Why My Church Does Not Sing Songs by Bethel, Elevation, and Hillsong A La Carte (May 15) Weekend A La Carte (July 15)
content: A few weeks ago, I explained why my church does not sing songs by Hillsong , and, by the same convictions, songs by Bethel and Elevation. I tried to be clear that I do not understand this to be a matter of clear right or wrong, but rather a matter of wisdom and conscience. While this is a decision we have made for our church, I would not look down on churches that choose differently. I wish I had addressed a related matter at that time: what should you do if you see this issue in the way I do, but the leaders of your church do not? In other words, what should you do if your church sings Hillsong, but you wish it wouldn’t? I want to offer just a few thoughts on that. In general, I would suggest you just sing the songs, provided they do not require you to sing anything that is unbiblical. And thankfully, the majority of the songs by Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation will not force you to sing error. That said, there are a few songs that may come close, or whose lyrics are imprecise enough that they could be understood in different ways. For example, Hillsong’s “So Will I (100 Billion X)” has these words in its second verse and the chorus that follows it: All nature and science Follow the sound of Your voice And as you speak A hundred billion creatures catch your breath Evolving in pursuit of what you said If it all reveals your nature so will I The most natural reading of those words is an affirmation of some kind of theistic evolution. I could not sing that, and I understand that you may not be able to either. Bethel’s “Reckless Love” continually ascribes recklessness to God. Oh, the overwhelming, never-ending, reckless love of God Oh, it chases me down, fights ’til I’m found, leaves the ninety-nine I couldn’t earn it, I don’t deserve it, still You give Yourself away Oh, the overwhelming, never-ending, reckless love of God It is difficult for me ( and for John Piper , as it happens) to find a sense in which the word “reckless” is a fitting word for God. I think I know what the songwriters were hoping to convey with the word, but “reckless” is not suitable when speaking of God’s love and purposes, and I understand why many Christians could simply not permit themselves to sing it. I couldn’t either. But apart from those songs and a few others, most do not contain lyrics that are false or wrong. If your elders have deemed these songs suitable for your church, then it’s probably best to sing them in submission to the people whose leadership you have decided to follow. There is no “followership” in this world, other than following Christ, that does not at times involve submitting our own preferences to the preferences of our leaders. It would probably be a good time for a reminder that you just can’t have it all on this side of glory. Every pastor, every eldership, and every church will have both strengths and weaknesses. Too many Christians (who are also a bewildering collection of both strengths and weaknesses, of course) spend their whole lives searching for a perfect church, never quite grasping that it’s a futile effort. They go to the church with great preaching, but find that its evangelism is disappointing; they head for the church with great evangelism, but find its polity is poor. They soon switch again, this time choosing the church with their preferred polity, only to discover that it’s lacking in fellowship. They never learn the joy of settling into an imperfect church, in which they can rejoice in the strengths while bearing with the weaknesses. Sometimes accepting those weaknesses means singing songs or tolerating musical styles that are not aligned with their preferences, even when that’s hard to do. But what if the church does sing those songs that have actual errors in them? In the moment, I’d suggest you simply stop singing and refrain from making a big deal of it. You don’t need to make a fuss or storm out. But afterward, it would be wise to speak with your pastors to address your concerns, humbly, of course, and w

title: A La Carte (November 9)
summary: Christianity under the progressive gaze / Why Christians must reject the conspiratorial mind / Wise people strive to be wiser / The pro-life movement’s midterm reckoning / How evil works / Preaching in paragraphs / Kindle deals / and more. See Also A La Carte (September 10) A La Carte (February 10) A La Carte (January 15)
content: Good morning. Grace and peace to you. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include several excellent biographies from Crossway. Each of them is good, but I’m partial to the one on R.C. Sproul. Note that these biographies are typically priced between $22 and $40. In case you missed it on the weekend, Westminster Books is offering a deep discount on the new graphic novel adaptation of Pilgrim’s Progress . Recommended Reading Christianity Under the Progressive Gaze. Kyle Borg: “What interests me more than politics is the apparent cultural strength and growing respectability of progressive Christianity. In fact, a headline in The Guardian boldly declared: ‘A progressive understanding of Christianity won in the US elections.’ In a society where historic Christian convictions — and I don’t just mean Reformed confessionalism but basic creedal Christianity — is often treated with suspicion, if not hostility, some expressions of ‘Christianity’ seem to be enjoying a rather warm reception.” Counterfeit Providence: Why Christians Must Reject the Conspiratorial Mind. Mitchell Bahnsen explores the conspiratorial mind and explains why it’s so important for Christians to reject it. “None of this requires Christians to become gullible or naive. Psalm 2 describes kings taking counsel together against the Lord, and the crucifixion itself was a conspiracy carried out jointly by religious and governmental authorities. True connivance does occur, and wisdom to discern the truth is necessary in a complex and fallen world. However, we must defend against a totalizing hermeneutic of suspicion, lest it become its own form of faith.” Wise People Strive To Be Wiser. Justin Huffman discusses a principle that may be obvious, but is also important. “The wise person is always seeking to become wiser still. The truly spiritual person recognizes his or her constant need for spiritual growth.” The Pro-Life Movement’s Midterm Reckoning. First Things allows everyone to access several free articles per month, and this one from Jonathon Van Maren is worth one of the quota. He considers how the battle against abortion is likely to look very different after the midterm elections. “‘It’s impossible to sugarcoat it,’ Marjorie Dannenfelser of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America wrote in a memo issued on November 3. The 2026 midterm election results ‘are a disaster for the unborn, for their mothers, and for the country as a whole. Democrats are on track to control two of the three pieces they need to legalize taxpayer-funded abortion on demand, up until birth, in all fifty states—something they promise to start pushing as soon as they take office in January.'” How Evil Works. John Piper helpfully explains how evil works. “At the center of Satan’s purpose is to deceive on earth and to accuse in heaven. If he can deceive you about God and Christ, you will perish. If he can successfully accuse you of unforgiven sin in heaven, you will perish. And Jesus calls him ‘a murderer from the beginning’ (John 8:44). So, the deception and the accusation and the eternal death that results from unforgiven sin is a way of destroying people and opposing God.” Preaching in Paragraphs. This may be helpful for preachers to read as they let last week’s sermon fade into the past and begin to think about the next one. “Every preacher knows the terror of a blank screen. It is Tuesday morning—or even worse, Saturday afternoon—and the preacher sits and stares at his laptop. He has opened a new document in his word processor, and now the cursor stands idling on the page, patiently blinking. And the words aren’t coming.” Reader Recommendations Once a week, I like to ask what you enjoy and recommend. What books, products, videos, sites, or other experiences do you recommend to others who read this blog/newsletter? Let me know, and I’ll share a collection on Saturday. (If you’re reading this via email, you’ll need to visit my site to fill out the form. Go here to read last week’s recommendations.) Submit

title: Works & Wonders (November 8)
summary: This week’s Works & Wonders: the power of God, Nikon’s microscope photos, three Come, Thou Founts, a brain-injured musical genius, and Prepare Him Room live. See Also Works & Wonders: October 25 Works & Wonders (July 19) Works & Wonders (May 10)
content: In my weekly Works & Wonders column, I combine a brief devotional with other interesting and uplifting bits and pieces I gleaned throughout the week. I hope you enjoy this week’s collection! It includes: His Will Will Be Done Photomicrography Come, Thou Fount (×3) The Brain-Injured Musical Genius Grain from an Attic Prepare Him Room (Live) 1. His Will Will Be Done To have power is to have ability and strength. This is true whether the power belongs to human beings or to God himself—to creatures or to the Creator. Of course, our power is derived from God’s, but his is inherent. We are accountable to God for the way we use our power, but God is accountable only to himself. Our power is always small and incomplete, but God’s is always unbounded and unlimited. To say we are powerful is to say we possess the ability to do some of the things we desire some of the time. But to say God is powerful is to say God always possesses within himself the means necessary to bring about whatsoever he wills—to execute all his plans, to execute them all the way to perfect completion, and to overcome any and all resistance. This guarantees that God’s will will be done, for as the psalmist says, “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases” (Psalm 115:3). The God we worship today is the God for whom this is true: Whatever his will resolves and however his wisdom directs, his power will accomplish. 2. Photomicrography Shall we look at the results of another photography competition? Why yes, we shall. This week it’s Nikon’s Photomicrography Competition . “What is photomicrography you ask” (other than a word that is almost impossible to type correctly the first time, or even the fourth, in my case)? It is taking photos of microscopic objects and, in that way, opening a view to a world that is otherwise far too small for us to see. I think you’ll enjoy browsing the winners, which include spiders, pens, neurons, and inkjet printers. 3. Come, Thou Fount (×3) I really enjoy The National Parks and their delightful, easy-to-listen-to folk-Americana music. It’s my understanding that they grew up Mormon but have spoken openly about leaving that faith, but I am not aware of them becoming Christian. I was surprised, then, to see they had released a version of “ Come, Thou Fount .” It’s quite a good one. I’m not sure what motivated them to record it, but perhaps it was the same thing that motivated Marcus Mumford of Mumford & Sons, who has also recorded and performed it several times—I assume it was just the sheer beauty of the song. Mumford was raised in a Christian home, though later left the faith. His version is also wonderful. Another favorite rendition, sung by Christians, is this one by Celtic Worship . 4. The Brain-Injured Musical Genius The New York Times had an amazing feature this week, and it was amazing in two ways. First, it was beautifully put together with animated graphics and other visual elements. Second, it told a remarkable story—the story of a man who suffered a terrible brain injury but, through it, became a musical genius. I think you’ll enjoy reading The Brain Injury That Made a Middle School Teacher a Musical Genius . 5. Grain from an Attic Here’s a fun story from Italy that pastors may want to hang on to for future sermon illustrations. In the early 1990s, a farmer in Parma found some old seeds in his attic. He assumed they were useless, so he tossed them on the manure pile. Much to his surprise, they sprouted into a form of grain he had never seen before. I’ll leave you to read the story, look at the pictures, and consider the many possible illustrations and applications. Photo credit: Clara Vannucci 6. Prepare Him Room (Live) A couple of days ago, a friend told me that his children had begun listening to Christmas music, and we discussed whether it’s still too early in the year for that. We agreed that you don’t want to begin listening too early lest you grow tired of the relatively limited catalog of songs before Christma

summary: God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sen
content: Participants at the IMB Sending Celebration on Nov. 9, 2026, celebrated God's faithfulness in sending 33 new missionaries to the nations. Held at the Sugarcreek campus of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, the event launched the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio annual gathering. For security reasons, some newly appointed missionaries are not publicly identified. IMB Photo God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sending and sustaining those called by God to go to the mission field. Senior Pastor Chad Keck welcomed those in attendance, sharing his appreciation for the partnership with Southern Baptist churches to cooperatively send and support missionaries. The Sending Celebration is meeting in conjunction with the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio. Chad Keck, senior pastor of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, left, and Jeremy Westbrook, executive director-treasurer of the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio, right, welcome guests gathered for the IMB Sending Celebration, which kicked off the convention’s annual gathering. IMB Photo Among those who shared their stories include a couple who answered an unexpected call later in life, a couple who are returning to Albania and to people they could not forget; and a couple who moved from welcoming the nations in Canada to going to Fiji. All of them shared their stories before the Sending Celebration. Unexpected invitation to go On Dec. 5, 2025, what seemed like an ordinary FaceTime call became a turning point for Rob Boss. As he spoke with his daughter, Hannah, during her IMB training, Rob sensed God speaking clearly to his heart: “You can do this too.” The impression was unexpected. After decades of writing, Christian education, seminary teaching and active support of missions, overseas service had never been part of Rob and Stephanie Boss’ plans. “It wasn’t an audible voice, but it was so clear,” Rob said. “It was Him. It was so kind and so gentle and so encouraging.” The moment drove him to his knees in surrender. When Stephanie came home later that day, he told her he believed God was calling them to the nations. Her response was immediate. “Thrilled is the right answer,” she said. The next day, the couple contacted the IMB and began the application process. Though missions had long been part of their family’s story, Rob and Stephanie Boss sensed God leading them to overseas service while encouraging their daughter, Hannah, during her missionary training. Sent by Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, Texas, they are now headed to Colombia, where they will serve through theological education. IMB Photo Looking back, the Bosses see the Lord’s hand preparing them long before they realized where He was leading. “God brought us together in the summer of 1990 at Glorieta, New Mexico, where we met and married,” Stephanie said during the Sending Celebration. What followed was years of ministry, teaching, parenting and navigating life’s unexpected turns, which taught them to hold plans loosely and trust God completely. “We did not have a clue about what life held in front of us,” Stephanie said. “We just knew we wanted to follow the Lord.” Their calling also continues a family legacy. Rob’s mother served with the IMB in Africa after retirement, helping inspire Hannah’s service in South Korea. Now, three generations of the same family have answered God’s call to the nations. Rob and Stephanie expressed deep gratitude for their sending church, Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, whose strong commitment to missions

title: IMB missionaries in place, prepared to encourage Senegal’s churches toward Youth Olympics outreach
summary: As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is exting
content: A Senegalese Christian shares the gospel with event volunteers during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is extinguished. “This is the first Olympic event ever held on the continent of Africa,” West said. “For us, it was an opportunity to ask, ‘What are we going to do with this?’” The Youth Olympic Games, which began Oct. 31 and end Nov. 13, are taking place across three host cities: Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. Event organizers expect nearly 2,700 athletes, ages 14-17, to participate in 35 sports and represent more than 200 delegations. The Games have drawn a million spectators, and West reported more than 6,000 event volunteers are staffing all the venues. With so many people gathering in Senegal, West and his team concentrated on preparing Senegalese churches for evangelistic opportunities. “We could run and hide, or we could do this thing,” West said, recalling an early conversation with teammates. “We decided we were going to do this thing.” The 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, is the first Olympic event held on the continent of Africa. IMB Photo West serves as team leader for IMB work in Senegal, where ministry efforts focus on three areas: gospel engagement, church advancement and community development. The Youth Olympic outreach naturally aligns with the first two priorities. “Our approach has been to mobilize the local church,” he said. “This is their backyard.” Instead of relying on a large influx of international volunteers, though there is one volunteer team from the United States serving, the strategy has centered on equipping local believers. Senegal has four Baptist churches in the greater Dakar area. Many leaders representing the congregations, as well as other ministry partners, participated in evangelism training designed specifically for the Games. Church leaders and ministry partners in Senegal participate in an evangelism training session specifically designed to share the gospel during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo A key outreach method involves trading commemorative pins, a familiar Olympic tradition. Volunteers use the exchange as a natural conversation starter before offering gospel-centered materials. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code connected to a digital engagement platform adapted from previous Olympic and World Cup outreaches. Visitors who scan the code are directed to online resources and can connect with trained digital responders. Experienced volunteers in the U.S. are helping provide follow-up conversations. “We’re building on strategies that have been used effectively in previous Olympic Games,” West said. “It’s an easy, non-intimidating way to start gospel conversations.” Trading commemorative pins is an Olympic tradition. Volunteers use these pins to start gospel-driven conversations during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code that connects people to trained digital responders. IMB Photo The effort extends beyond Dakar. IMB teams and church partners are positioned in each of the three host cities. An IMB team, which includes three global missionary partners, is helping coordinate outreach efforts in Diamniadio, and an IMB team along with a Baptist church is organizing efforts in Saly. West believes the greatest potential impact may be felt not among international visitors but among Senegalese believers themselves. Senegal is approximately 95% Muslim and 0.2% evangelical. He called on the nation to accomplish this within a decade. This extraordinary, demanding, costly endeavor is known to history as Kennedy’s “moon shot.” The nation rose to the challenge.
